Parts, labor, tax, total. The invoice is the most precise document in the whole repair process and the least informative.

What it does not show is the 40 minutes your coordinator spent on hold, the two days the estimate sat unread, the three line items priced above your matrix that nobody had time to check, or the comeback in six weeks for the same complaint. Those costs are real, they are recurring, and they are measurable. Most fleets simply do not measure them.
This is the cost of the repair process itself, separate from the cost of the vehicle being off the road. Both matter. This one is the cheaper of the two to fix.

The estimate arrives. Someone has to read it, check it against policy and warranty, decide, and tell the shop. Every hour between arrival and answer is an hour the vehicle is parked and the bay is idle. This is the single most controllable number in the whole process and the one fleets track least, because it lives in an inbox rather than a system.
Approval latency. Median hours from estimate received to estimate approved or rejected. Track the median and the 90th percentile, because the tail is where the damage is.
Estimate-to-invoice variance. Final invoice minus approved estimate, divided by approved estimate. Report it per shop, as a median and as a 90th percentile.
First-pass approval rate. Estimates approved without a revision request, divided by all estimates. A low rate means your policy is not reaching the shop before the estimate is written.

Comeback rate. Repair orders reopened for the same complaint within 30 days, divided by repair orders closed. Anything you cannot attribute to a specific shop is a data problem, not a quality problem.
